data.title: Why Hims & Hers Health Fell 52% Even As Sales Rose
data.description:

For Hims & Hers Health shareholders, the loss over the past year was 52.4%, including dividends. The Two Stories Hims & Hers Health Investors Were Weighing

The shares cost US$36.26 at the start of the period, and you had to decide which story about Hims & Hers Health felt more convincing.

On the upbeat side, one thesis saw telehealth and hormonal care reshaping global markets, with a Fair Value of US$47.42, a price level implied by assumptions like 18.8% revenue growth and an 8.1% profit margin over three years.

The more cautious view put Fair Value at US$28, a lower implied price that stressed rising regulatory costs, tougher telehealth competition, and pressure on pricing power as key risks.

What The Hims & Hers Health Results Put To The Test

The big development was Hims & Hers Health closing the Eucalyptus deal and pushing hard into GLP-1 and peptide therapies, which lined up with the bullish story about global reach and broader treatment categories. Q3 2026 results told a different part of the story. Revenue rose to US$890.4m, but profit turned into a US$33.0m loss and net margin fell to -3.7%, so the profitability piece of the upbeat case stayed unproven. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The lesson is simple. When a business leans on scale and new categories to justify optimism, track whether higher sales are turning into a healthier net margin. A Closer Look At Finatext Holdings' Earnings

In high finance, the key ratio used to measure how well a company converts reported profits into free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio (from cashflow). The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Finatext Holdings has an accrual ratio of 0.27 for the year to September 2026. Unfortunately, that means its free cash flow fell significantly short of its reported profits. Over the last year it actually had negative free cash flow of JP¥331m, in contrast to the aforementioned profit of JP¥1.79b. We also note that Finatext Holdings' free cash flow was actually negative last year as well, so we could understand if shareholders were bothered by its outflow of JP¥331m.

You could think of the accrual ratio from cashflow as the 'non-FCF profit ratio'.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

For the year to September 2026, Decollte Holdings had an accrual ratio of -0.20. That implies it has very good cash conversion, and that its earnings in the last year actually significantly understate its free cash flow. To wit, it produced free cash flow of JP¥1.7b during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of JP¥288.0m. Decollte Holdings shareholders are no doubt pleased that free cash flow improved over the last twelve months.
